The benefits everyone talks about — better sleep, less anxiety, manifesting what you want — aren't actually why you meditate. They're just the side effects.

The real target has a name most people have never heard: samskaras, energetic imprints sitting in your field, running 24 hours a day, 7 days a week, as a counter-intention to everything you're trying to build. They're not symbolic. They're actively working against your own goals in the background, whether you're aware of them or not.

His real name wasn't Osho. It was Bhagwan Rajneesh, and before the name change, he ran a commune in Oregon with 97 Rolls-Royces parked outside it.

People got murdered there. It became one of the stranger chapters in American spiritual history — documented now on Netflix — and the man at the center of it still has meditation techniques people practice today. The teaching can be real and useful. The teacher can still be a cautionary tale. Those aren't in conflict.

He meditated every single day for decades — twenty minutes, twice a day, no exceptions. During his seven months alone in a cave, that became eight hours a day.

Here's what almost nobody tells you about what happens after years of that: meditation stops being a technique you perform and becomes a state you're simply in. Eating becomes meditation. Driving becomes meditation. Even intimacy becomes meditation. Not because you're trying — because there's nothing left pulling you out of the present moment.

Go to any airport, any DMV, any waiting room, and watch. Nobody is just sitting there anymore.

Everyone needs a screen, a phone, a TV bolted to the wall — anything to avoid being alone with their own mind for ninety seconds. That restlessness isn't a personality trait. It's a signal. The more agitated you feel in silence, the more active imprints you're carrying, and the more meditation — not less — is actually what you need.

clips.end_words: one of your buttons are being pushed
clips.caption:
A stranger spits in your face. You get angry, maybe even take a swing. That's rational — proportional to what just happened to you.

A car horn beeps and you want to scream and chase the driver down. That's not rational, and that's the tell: a button just got pushed, an old, stored imprint surfacing as rage that has nothing to do with the horn. Meditation is what's supposed to find those buttons on purpose, before life finds them for you.

People hear stories about meditation retreats, hallucinations, twelve-hour days, and think more must be better. It isn't, not for you, not yet.

Push past twenty minutes, twice a day, and you hit a wall fast: three extra hours buys you roughly two percent more benefit. The people doing marathon sessions spent years at the basic practice first. Skipping to the deep end doesn't get you there faster. It just means you're meditating wrong, longer.
